item.title: Singh queries missing FICAC complaint file
item.description: A FILE containing a complaint against a former Fiji Sugar Corporation senior official allegedly went missing after it was lodged with the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption about three-and-a-half years ago. This was the revelation made by incoming Sugar Minister Charan Jeath Singh during a recent interview with this newspaper at Mata-i-Labasa in Macuata.
item.content:encoded:
A FILE containing a complaint against a former Fiji Sugar Corporation senior official allegedly went missing after it was lodged with the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption about three-and-a-half years ago.

This was the revelation made by incoming Sugar Minister Charan Jeath Singh during a recent interview with this newspaper at Mata-i-Labasa in Macuata.

Mr Singh said a complaint had been lodged with FICAC over what he described as an alleged corrupt deal involving the former executive.

“We had made a complaint about three-and-a-half years ago to FICAC, however, they had stated that the file went missing,” he said.

He said another file was subsequently prepared, but no charges had been laid.

If FICAC maintained that the original file was still missing, Mr Singh said another copy of the complaint and supporting documents could be provided.

He alleged that transactions had been identified in the senior officers overseas bank account, with money allegedly being transferred from Hong Kong and other parts of the world.

FICAC was approached for clarification on the complaint and its current status, however, questions to the organisation remain unanswered.

item.title: Muslim community integral to Fiji’s national journey – PM Rabuka
item.description: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has acknowledged the longstanding contribution of Fiji’s Muslim community to the country’s development, saying Muslims have been an integral part of the nation’s journey across generations. item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has acknowledged the longstanding contribution of Fiji’s Muslim community to the country’s development, saying Muslims have been an integral part of the nation’s journey across generations.

In his national address marking the Birthday of the Holy Prophet Muhammad, Mr Rabuka paid tribute to the contribution of Muslim Fijians in education, agriculture, business, the professions, public service and charitable work.

“The Muslim community has long been an integral part of Fiji’s national journey,” Mr Rabuka said.

“Across generations, Muslim Fijians have contributed immensely to our nation’s development — in education, agriculture, commerce, the professions, public service, charitable work and community development.”

He said Muslim organisations and individuals continued to provide services extending beyond their own religious community.

“Many Muslim organisations and individuals continue to serve not only members of their own faith, but Fijians from every community,” he said.

“Their commitment to faith, family, and service continues to make a meaningful and lasting contribution to the wellbeing and progress of our country.”

Mr Rabuka said this commitment reflected an important message from the occasion — that faith could be demonstrated through service to others.

“That spirit of service reflects one of the most important lessons we can take from this occasion: that our faith is expressed most meaningfully through the good that we do for others,” he said.

The Prime Minister also called for greater respect between Fiji’s different religious and cultural communities.

He said the country was strengthened by its diversity and should remain a place where no person felt less Fijian because of religion, ethnicity, language or cultural background.

“A Fiji where our children grow up understanding that diversity does not weaken a nation — division does,” Mr Rabuka said.

He said the responsibility of all Fijians was to ensure the bonds uniting the country remained stronger than its differences.

“We are a country of diverse communities, but we share one Fiji and one future,” he said.

Mr Rabuka wished Muslims in Fiji and around the world peace, joy and blessings on the occasion of Eid Milad-un-Nabi.

item.title: Prof Prasad praises Muslim League’s century of service
item.description: National Federation Party leader Prof Biman Prasad has praised the Fiji Muslim League for its contribution to Fiji over the past century, saying the Muslim community has played an important role in the country’s religious, social, economic and political development. Prof Prasad extended his greetings to Fiji’s Muslim community on the occasion of the Birthday of the Holy Prophet Muhammad, which thi
item.content:encoded:
National Federation Party leader Prof Biman Prasad has praised the Fiji Muslim League for its contribution to Fiji over the past century, saying the Muslim community has played an important role in the country’s religious, social, economic and political development.

Prof Prasad extended his greetings to Fiji’s Muslim community on the occasion of the Birthday of the Holy Prophet Muhammad, which this year coincides with the Fiji Muslim League’s 100th anniversary.

“For a century, the Fiji Muslim League has been an important part of Fiji’s religious, educational and social development,” he said.

He said the League’s schools, community institutions, charitable work and advocacy had made a lasting contribution to Fiji.

He also highlighted the contribution of former NFP leader and Leader of the Opposition Siddiq Moidin Koya, particularly his role in securing national recognition for the Birthday of the Holy Prophet Muhammad and Diwali as public holidays in 1974.

Prof Prasad said the decision was an example of political dialogue and bipartisanship recognising Fiji’s religious and cultural diversity.

He said the NFP remained committed to its founding principle that every community should have an equal place in Fiji’s national life.

“Our diversity should strengthen our national community and deepen our respect and understanding for one another.”

He congratulated the Fiji Muslim League on its 100 years of service and wished Muslims in Fiji and around the world a peaceful and meaningful observance of the Birthday of the Holy Prophet Muhammad.

item.title: Great Council of Chiefs to get a seat on FNU Council
item.description: The Great Council of Chiefs could have representation on the governing Council of the Fiji National University under proposed legislation tabled in Parliament last week. The Fiji National University Bill 2026 provides for the Minister responsible, after consultation with the FNU Council, to appoint up to three co-opted members to the Council.
item.content:encoded:
The Great Council of Chiefs could have representation on the governing Council of the Fiji National University under proposed legislation tabled in Parliament last week.

The Fiji National University Bill 2026 provides for the Minister responsible, after consultation with the FNU Council, to appoint up to three co-opted members to the Council.

Under Clause 21 of the Bill, a person would be eligible for appointment as a co-opted member if nominated by the Great Council of Chiefs, or if the person represents one of several specified organisations.

These include the Fiji Teachers Union or Fiji Teachers Association, Fiji Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation.

The provision potentially gives the Great Council of Chiefs a formal avenue to nominate a person for consideration for appointment to the governing body of one of Fiji’s major tertiary institutions.

Co-opted members would serve a three-year term, beginning from the first scheduled Council meeting following their appointment.

Their appointment could be renewed for another term on the recommendation of the FNU Council.

item.title: Vosarogo tells Nath: ‘You are not coming back’
item.description: A brief political exchange drew attention in Parliament on Friday after Minister for Lands and Mineral Resources Filimoni Vosarogo told Opposition MP Vijay Nath, “You are not coming back.” The remark came as Mr Nath questioned the Minister for Immigration, Viliame Naupoto about plans to expand online government services for people living in Fiji’s rural and maritime communities.
item.content:encoded:
A brief political exchange drew attention in Parliament on Friday after Minister for Lands and Mineral Resources Filimoni Vosarogo told Opposition MP Vijay Nath, “You are not coming back.”

The remark came as Mr Nath questioned the Minister for Immigration, Viliame Naupoto about plans to expand online government services for people living in Fiji’s rural and maritime communities.

Mr Nath said people in remote areas deserved better access to government services and questioned whether commitments outlined by the Minister could be delivered within the remaining months of the parliamentary term.

“We look forward to whatever he has mentioned is able to be fulfilled in these four months because their term is about to finish, otherwise, we have to come back and do it,” Mr Nath said.

Mr Vosarogo responded: “You are not coming back.”

The exchange also brought an election flavour to the parliamentary proceedings.

item.title: Up to $6M for mills upgrade annually
item.description: Sugar factories are spending between $3 million and $6 million annually for maintenance as the industry grapples with ageing mills and declining sugarcane production, according to the Ministry of Sugar Industry. The figures were provided in the Ministry’s response to questions from Parliament’s Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defence during its review of the Ministry of Sugar Industry’s
item.content:encoded:
Sugar factories are spending between $3 million and $6 million annually for maintenance as the industry grapples with ageing mills and declining sugarcane production, according to the Ministry of Sugar Industry.

The figures were provided in the Ministry’s response to questions from Parliament’s Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defence during its review of the Ministry of Sugar Industry’s 2020-2021 Annual Report.

The Ministry said factories were currently spending approximately $3 million to $6 million every year in relation to ageing mill infrastructure.

The disclosure comes as production figures show continuing pressure on an industry that remains an important part of Fiji’s economy.

According to figures submitted to the committee, Fiji produced 1.73 million tonnes of sugarcane in 2020, resulting in 152,000 tonnes of sugar.

Cane production dropped to 1.42 million tonnes in 2021, while sugar production fell to 133,000 tonnes.

In 2023, 1.57 million tonnes of cane produced 140,000 tonnes of sugar, while production declined to 1.33 million tonnes of cane and 126,000 tonnes of sugar in 2024.

Sugar production was listed at 110,000 tonnes in 2025.

The Ministry also outlined measures aimed at addressing declining farmer numbers and the movement of young people away from the industry.

It said existing and new farmers were being supported through cane planting grants, fertiliser and weedicide subsidies, assistance with lease renewal costs and grants for adopting new technology.

Subsidies are also available for mechanical harvesters, planters and fertiliser applicators.

The Ministry said cheaper loan financing was being offered to help establish sugarcane farms.

Other initiatives include promoting voluntary Fiji National Provident Fund schemes among farmers to improve retirement savings.

Farmers are also covered through a micro-bundled insurance scheme, while some have taken up parametric insurance to provide protection against climate-related events.

The Ministry’s response highlights the financial challenge of maintaining ageing milling infrastructure while simultaneously trying to reverse falling production and attract a new generation of farmers.

item.title: Up to 12,000 people could be living with HIV in Fiji
item.description: As many as 12,000 people could be living with HIV in Fiji, as the country confronts a generalised epidemic and continues to record rising infections, Health Minister Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu told Parliament last week. Dr Ratu Lalabalavu said 2026 UNAIDS estimates indicated about 9100 people were living with HIV in 2025, but the actual figure could be considerably higher.
item.content:encoded:
As many as 12,000 people could be living with HIV in Fiji, as the country confronts a generalised epidemic and continues to record rising infections, Health Minister Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu told Parliament last week.

Dr Ratu Lalabalavu said 2026 UNAIDS estimates indicated about 9100 people were living with HIV in 2025, but the actual figure could be considerably higher.

“Let me be direct with this House that Fiji is now in a generalised HIV epidemic,” he said.

“2026 UNAIDS estimates indicate that about 9,100 people were living with HIV in 2025 and possibly as many as 12,000, up from fewer than 700 in 2010.”

He said HIV prevalence among adults aged 15 to 49 had reached 1.6 per cent, crossing the threshold defining a generalised epidemic.

An estimated 1700 new infections occurred in 2025, around three times the level recorded in 2018.

“I will not stand before this House and claim that we have already turned the curve downward,” Dr Lalabalavu said.

“The honest position is that we have not yet reached the turning point.”

Despite the figures, he said progress was being made in identifying people living with HIV.

The number of people who knew their HIV status increased from about 785 in 2022 to 3551 in 2025, while the number receiving treatment grew from around 506 in 2020 to more than 2000 last year.

Dr Lalabalavu stressed the importance of achieving viral suppression.

“A person who is virally suppressed cannot pass HIV. Let me repeat that. A person who is virally suppressed cannot pass HIV,” he said.

“Treatment is therefore also prevention.”

However, he acknowledged Fiji could not yet reliably measure viral suppression nationwide and said improvements to viral-load testing were part of the response.

Dr Lalabalavu also highlighted needle and syringe sharing associated with high-risk drug use as a significant factor in Fiji’s rapid increase in HIV infections.

“The global evidence is clear. The harm reduction programme, including a Needle Syringe Programme, is urgently needed to interrupt this route of transmission,” he said.

The Ministry is working with the law and justice sector on regulations to allow the safe and lawful introduction of harm-reduction programmes, which Dr Lalabalavu said would be scaled up as a priority once regulations were in place.

item.title: Ditoka: Diplomatic relationships cannot be switched off
item.description: The cost of withdrawing Fiji’s diplomatic presence from key international capitals cannot always be entered neatly into a spreadsheet, Foreign Affairs Minister Sakiasi Ditoka told Parliament last week. Mr Ditoka made the comments while reflecting on Fiji’s decision during the COVID-19 period to step back from its diplomatic presence in Kuala Lumpur, Seoul and Brussels.
item.content:encoded:
The cost of withdrawing Fiji’s diplomatic presence from key international capitals cannot always be entered neatly into a spreadsheet, Foreign Affairs Minister Sakiasi Ditoka told Parliament last week.

Mr Ditoka made the comments while reflecting on Fiji’s decision during the COVID-19 period to step back from its diplomatic presence in Kuala Lumpur, Seoul and Brussels.

“There is a cost, Mr Speaker, Sir, that cannot always be entered neatly into a spreadsheet,” he said.

“Relationships cool, institutional connections weaken, opportunities are missed, and partners can reasonably begin to ask whether Fiji still values the relationship the same way they do.”

Mr Ditoka said diplomatic relationships required continuous attention and could not simply be suspended and expected to resume years later from where they had stopped.

“In both capitals, we were disappointed that Fiji had stepped back from relationships our partners continued to value,” he said.

“These were friendships, and they are still friendships built over many years, and our partners had invested considerable goodwill in Fiji.”

Mr Ditoka acknowledged the severe economic and fiscal pressures Fiji faced during COVID-19 but questioned why the strategic approach taken to preserve Fiji Airways had not also been applied to diplomatic missions.

He credited the former government for recognising Fiji Airways as a strategic national asset despite pressure facing the airline during the pandemic.

“On that principle, they were right,” he said.

“However, it does also raise a legitimate question. Why was the same strategic thinking not applied to Fiji’s diplomatic presence in Kuala Lumpur, Seoul and Brussels?”

Mr Ditoka said Malaysia was at the heart of ASEAN, Seoul was the capital of a major global economy and longstanding development partner, while Brussels was central to Fiji’s engagement with the European Union and important trade and development relationships.

“COVID itself does not remove the strategic importance of diplomatic relationships,” he said.

“Diplomacy does not cease because aircraft stop flying. Indeed, periods of international crisis occur precisely when relationships between countries matter the most.”
